sections.name: Top stories
sections.label: Top stories
sections.glance: Nvidia agrees to buy the Hugging Face Hub; Ox Alpha turns out to be GLM-5.3-Flash; two harness papers in two days; Nvidia's quarter; a hundred companies on AI-enabled attacks.
sections.lead: Five stories about who controls the layers around a model. Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face, the default place open weights are published, and the one open-weight launch of the week, Z.ai's GLM-5.3-Flash, turned out to be the anonymous Ox Alpha that had been collecting third-party scores. Two papers made the harness itself the thing that learns: Prime Agent keeps its memories, skills and prompts across attempts, JIT-Agent writes a harness for each task. Nvidia's quarter (corrected below: $96.2 billion, not $92 billion) says the spending under all of it has not slowed, and more than a hundred companies, the labs among them, signed a call to defend against attacks those same agents make easier.

sections.name: Models & releases
sections.label: Models
sections.glance: Three open-weight MoEs (GLM-5.3-Flash, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Tencent Hy4), a diffusion drafter, Cohere's page parser, Nvidia's FP4 builds, and OpenAI's workbench, leak and retirements. Holds the drafting animation and the parameter counter.
sections.lead: Three Chinese labs shipped open-weight mixtures of experts in one week: Z.ai's GLM-5.3-Flash (320B, 18B active), Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (125B, 6B active, previewing Qwen4) and Tencent's Hy4 preview (770B, 49B active), and Nvidia's 4-bit build of DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 followed two weeks after the original. Their headline counts and their checkpoints do not always agree, so the counter after the DeepSeek item counts each one every way and turns parameters into bytes. The serving story is DFlash2, which drafts a whole block of tokens in one pass for speculative decoding, animated against one-token-at-a-time drafting. The rest: Cohere Parse 5 sells pages, not scores; Claude Code gets a restricted mode; OpenAI ships a life-sciences workbench, retires the DALL-E GPT, tests a persistent Codex and has its next model leak.

sections.name: Research & papers
sections.label: Research
sections.glance: The harness papers in full (Prime Agent, JIT-Agent, WikiSkill, ContextPilot, Apodex), a double-blind evaluation, a science agent benchmark, OpenAI's incident report and Anthropic on automating its own research. Holds the skills-against-size chart.
sections.lead: The research week was about what an agent keeps between attempts. Prime Agent and JIT-Agent (summarised in [[Top stories|t-top|i-harness]]) and Google's WikiSkill all move learning out of the weights and into a persistent store or a generated harness; ContextPilot trains the model to manage its own context instead; Apodex 1.1 is the model-side answer, training coordination into the model. WikiSkill's full table is drawn below, because it holds the week's cleanest test of the claim that a smaller model with learned skills beats a larger one without. The measurement items ask what a score can be trusted for: DeepMind ran an evaluation where neither side sees the other's secrets, Terminal-Bench-Science puts agents on research workflows, and OpenAI and Anthropic each published what their own agents did, one by accident and one by design.

sections.name: Industry
sections.label: Industry
sections.glance: Open-weight companies as acquisition targets, AWS buys DuckDB's company but not DuckDB, OpenAI cuts Cursor off, a court strikes down the Pentagon's Anthropic ban, stolen Claude sessions, and the money.
sections.lead: The deals and the dependencies. TechCrunch's trend piece names the pattern behind [[Nvidia and Hugging Face|t-top|i-hf-deal]]: the distribution and routing layers for open models are being bought. AWS's purchase of DuckLabs shows a different structure, buying the company while the project stays in an independent foundation, and OpenAI's decision to stop serving Cursor after SpaceX bought it shows what a dependency on one supplier means. A federal judge ruled the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic unconstitutional, OpenAI is pricing some contracts by outcome, Big Tech's profits now include large paper gains on AI stakes, and Apple changes CEO. One security item lives here because it is a customer story: infostealers took Claude sessions, not passwords.

sections.name: Compute & chips
sections.label: Compute
sections.glance: AMD's Helios rack against Rubin, Nvidia selling the system rather than the chip, 15 GW that may sit dark in 2027, and the two numbers to carry from Nvidia's quarter.
sections.lead: The unit of competition moved from the chip to the rack and then to the site. AMD's Hot Chips figures are per 72-GPU rack (31 TB of HBM4, about 432 GB per GPU); Nvidia's pitch for Vera Rubin is the CPU, storage and networking around the GPU; and the binding constraint for 2027 may be transformers and grid connections, not silicon. The tab also carries the issue's two numbers from [[Nvidia's quarter|t-top|i-nvda-q]], corrected there, and a spot-price figure that no source could be found for.

sections.name: Dev tooling and agents
sections.label: Dev tools
sections.glance: Anthropic's Model Hardware Standard for lab equipment, vLLM v0.28.0, htmx 4.0 and Tailcat.
sections.lead: Four tools, two of them about agents reaching further. Anthropic's Model Hardware Standard lets an agent drive microscopes, liquid handlers and robot arms through MCP, a command line or code files; vLLM v0.28.0 is where this week's serving research lands, with [[DFlash2|t-models|i-dflash2]] drafting and DeepSeek-V4's sparse attention working end to end. htmx 4.0 and Tailcat were the week's most-upvoted developer stories on Hacker News.

sections.name: Security
sections.label: Security
sections.glance: Worms that run open-weight models on the machines they infect, and a Codex memory feature crossing a provider boundary (source now found).
sections.lead: Two items the backfill put under Security, and both are about a boundary an agent crosses without anyone deciding it should. A worm that brings its own open-weight model needs no API that can be revoked; a memory feature that summarises old chats can send a local provider's conversation to another provider. The week's other security items live where the issue put them: the [[joint call on AI-enabled attacks|t-top|i-cyber-call]], the [[stolen Claude sessions|t-industry|i-claude-sessions]], [[Grok's encrypted prompt injection|t-talk|i-grok-cci]] and [[OpenAI's Hugging Face incident|t-research|i-oai-incident]].

sections.name: Talk of the town
sections.label: Talk of the town
sections.glance: "MCP is dead", Grok's unpatched injection, the AI traffic numbers, the week's Hacker News threads and three essays. Holds the stateless MCP animation and the traffic check.
sections.lead: What people argued about. Two arguments had a mechanism under them, and both are drawn here: whether MCP without its session is just HTTP (animated: the same requests, before and after the 2026-07-28 revision), and whether "less traffic, better traffic" holds once the AI referrals are put on the same scale as the organic sessions they replace (they offset about a twentieth). Grok's encrypted injection shows why a code interpreter changes what a content filter can see. The rest is the week's attention: GLM and Qwen at the top of Hacker News, a study of the words Claude leans on, NPR's propaganda test, and three essays on agents, engineers and open models.

glance.label: At a glance
glance.lead: The second weekly digest, covering roughly 2026-08-25 to 2026-08-31: 60 items in eight sections, assembled from three parts (the issue as published, the items merged in from a second run of the same routine, and a backfill added after publication). Here the items are regrouped by subject, one tab per section, each card saying which part it came from; this tab is the week in one screen.
glance.theme: The week's theme: the layers around the model changed hands. The Hub where open weights are published is being bought by the company that sells the chips they run on ([[Top stories|t-top|i-hf-deal]]); OpenAI stopped supplying a rival's coding tool ([[Industry|t-industry|i-cursor]]); three harness papers made the scaffolding, not the weights, the part that learns ([[Research|t-research|v-wiki]]); and the week's security stories were all about something crossing a layer: a stolen session, an encrypted instruction a filter cannot read, a worm that brings its own model ([[Security|t-security]]). Two mechanisms changed underneath: drafting a block of tokens in one pass ([[animated in Models|t-models|v-dflash]]) and MCP without sessions ([[animated in Talk of the town|t-talk|v-mcp]]).
glance.next_title: What happened next, in one line each (as of 2026-10-02)
glance.parts_title: How this issue was put together
glance.parts_lead: The issue in Notion has three parts, written by two runs of the weekly routine and a review after publication. The cards in every tab are labelled with their part; the parts' own notes are kept here, verbatim.

notes: The gap was three or four days, not a week. Business Insider first reported the talks "over the weekend", in TechCrunch's words (the previous issue dates its pickup Aug 24), and The Information reported the agreement on Wednesday night, Aug 26 ({{TechCrunch|https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/26/nvidia-closes-in-on-hugging-face-acquisition/}}).

Checked 2026-10-02 against TechCrunch: the $12.9 billion is The Information's figure, citing one source; Business Insider said the talks valued Hugging Face at more than $13 billion, had not produced a signed agreement and "could still atomize"; neither company had replied, and TechCrunch makes the same point about Nvidia's silence. The 2023 round raised $235 million at $4.5 billion, so $12.9B is 2.87 times that (derived; "roughly 3x" holds). Hugging Face had turned down a $500 million Nvidia investment at a $7 billion valuation, and earns about $150 million a year (The Information, via TechCrunch).
The trend this deal fits is in [[Industry|t-industry|i-openweight-targets]]; the Stripe and OpenRouter deal is in the {{previous issue|n:3c65c17b0d0d81ca8c8af3c2fc0c3ced}}.

SiliconANGLE adds output of up to 131,072 tokens. Hugging Face lists 321.3B parameters in the checkpoint, almost all FP8 ({{zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash|https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash}}, created Aug 25).
Counted every way, with its bytes, in [[the parameter counter in Models|t-models|v-params]]; its Hacker News threads are in [[Talk of the town|t-talk|i-glm-hn]].

Prime Agent ({{arXiv 2608.23552|https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23552}}, submitted Aug 24) "raises ARC-AGI-3 RHAE Best@1 from 30% to 95.5%"; its Continual Harness preserves histories, memories, skills, prompts and subagent specifications across trajectories. JIT-Agent ({{arXiv 2608.25593|https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25593}}, v1 Aug 26, revised Sep 3) is JIT-Agent-27B, trained from Qwen3.6-27B; the nine-benchmark averages rise from 74.1 to 81.8 with GLM-5.2 (+7.7) and from 66.7 to 75.5 with DeepSeek-V4-Flash (+8.8), and per-case cost is 14.9 to 54.1% below the cheapest fixed harness (36.0% on average) in all six cost settings.

The third harness result of the fortnight, WikiSkill, is drawn in full in [[Research|t-research|v-wiki]]; the two papers' own entries are in [[Research|t-research|i-prime]]. The 30% baseline and AVO's 100% are in the {{previous issue|n:3c65c17b0d0d81ca8c8af3c2fc0c3ced}}.

notes: Two corrections. The card is published by Inco AI (the Hugging Face account incoai), not z-lab; z-lab's researchers (Chen, Liang and Liu) wrote the original DFlash, which the card cites. And this is not the first production use of text diffusion in serving: Inco's post says the original DFlash already runs in SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM and llama.cpp, is the default on CoreWeave's production Kimi K2.7 Code endpoint, and had more than 3.5 million downloads by August 2026 ({{Inco AI, DFlash 2|https://inco.ai/blog/dflash2/}}).

Checked 2026-10-02 against the card: SGLang on one H200, blocks of 8 (seven draft tokens per verification), Qwen3.8's recommended sampling at xhigh effort. "Up to 3.43x" is GSM8K at one request at a time (68.9 to 236.1 tokens per second); at 32 concurrent requests the gain is 1.01 to 1.45x, and Qwen3.8's built-in MTP drafter falls below plain decoding (0.77 to 1.04x). The drafter has 1.92B parameters. The selector keeps the top 16 candidates at each position and scores neighbouring pairs; two-tap convolutions hold accuracy toward the end of the block (Inco's post).
vLLM v0.28.0 added DFlash2 the same week ([[Dev tools|t-dev|i-vllm]]); DiffusionGemma, a model that decodes by diffusion itself, is in the {{previous issue|n:3c65c17b0d0d81ca8c8af3c2fc0c3ced}}.

Checked 2026-10-02 against InfoQ: the initialize and initialized exchange, the Mcp-Session-Id header and protocol sessions are gone from the request path; each request carries its protocol version, client identity and capabilities, so "any request can land on any instance". Two headers become mandatory, Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name, so a gateway can route, throttle and meter by method or tool without reading the body. Server-initiated requests become Multi Round-Trip Requests (the server returns input_required and the client retries), and Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated. MCP passed 400 million monthly SDK downloads.

22.dnote: Adversa's post; reported to xAI Jun 3
notes: Checked 2026-10-02 against Adversa (Aug 20): reported to xAI and its HackerOne programme on June 3, 2026, with further attempts on Aug 4 and 10 and no response; "As of August 19, we could still reproduce the attack against Grok." The payload is AES-256-GCM under a PBKDF2 key, opaque to a classifier although the key travels with it; the exfiltrated fields are the user's name, coarse location, subscription tier and the full set of prompts. June 3 to Aug 31 is 89 days, 12.7 weeks (derived), so "11+ weeks" holds.
The "about 40% over 20 attempts" is not in Adversa's post, and The Register's link returns 404 on 2026-10-02, so it could not be re-checked.

The issue gives no source. The data is Brainlabs' ({{Brainlabs|https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/why-organic-traffic-is-declining-ai-seo/}}), reported by {{Digiday|https://digiday.com/marketing/in-graphic-detail-how-ai-search-has-impacted-the-web-traffic-of-over-50-advertisers/}} on Aug 25.

Checked 2026-10-02: every figure is Brainlabs'. The comparison is the months before September 2025 (when about 30% of US desktop keywords triggered AI Overviews) against the eight months after, from Google Analytics data on 54 clients: organic sessions 140.1 million to 125.4 million (-10.5%), AI referrals up more than 163%, AI-driven key events up 335%. Over the period AI referrals converted at 13.4% against 10.4% for organic, about 1.5x by April 2026. Brainlabs' own caveat: organic fell by almost 14.7 million sessions and AI referrals rose by just under 800,000, "offsetting only around 5%".

125B is the language model without its n-gram embeddings. The card says "125B with 6B activated, plus 51B n-gram embedding and 4B MTP", and the checkpoint holds 180.0B parameters in BF16, 360 GB ({{Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next|https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next}}). Counted as weights to store, it is a 180B model.

The issue gives no source: {{NPR, Aug 30|https://www.npr.org/2026/08/30/nx-s1-5876436/chatbots-search-propaganda}}.

Checked 2026-10-02: NPR ran it with NewsGuard, 30 questions built on false narratives from China, Iran and Russia, against chatbots and search engines; chatbots "correctly debunked false narratives about three-quarters of the time"; the "look at the evidence" follow-up is Mike Caulfield's advice quoted in the piece.

Checked 2026-10-02 against Tencent: 770B total, 49B active, context over 1M; the blind evaluation (163 experts, 203 engineering tasks) gives 2.99 against GLM-5.3 2.92 and Kimi K3 2.94; free on WorkBuddy and CodeBuddy for two weeks; API $0.834 input and $2.501 output per million. The 31.8% is end-to-end inference throughput, from the model optimising its own inference system (operator fusion, communication); its part in training was proposing and running experiments on training methods, data, evaluation and operators. Hugging Face: {{tencent/Hy4-preview|https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy4-preview}} holds 779.96B parameters in BF16, 1.560 TB, which reproduces the "roughly 1.56TB" (779.96B x 2 bytes). Simon Willison's {{hands-on note|https://simonwillison.net/2026/Aug/29/hy4/}} (Aug 29): text input only.
The two reasoning levels and no_think are not in Tencent's post; the model card was not read.

The link points at a different checkpoint. {{nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-NVFP4|https://huggingface.co/nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-NVFP4}} quantises the original DeepSeek-V4-Pro and was created on May 14, 2026. The 0813 build is {{nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813-NVFP4|https://huggingface.co/nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813-NVFP4}}, created Aug 27, 14 days after DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 (Aug 13). AMD's NVFP4 build (amd/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-NVFP4, Jun 30) is also of the original, not of 0813.

Checked 2026-10-02 against the 0813 card: "ready for commercial or non-commercial use", quantised with Model Optimizer; only the linear layers in the MoE blocks are quantised (weights and activations). 1.6T total, 49B active. On Hugging Face it occupies 941 GB against 1,782 GB for DeepSeek's own 0813 repository (1.9x smaller, derived from the repositories' storage).

It is built on a domain model: OpenAI says Rosalind Workbench "builds on GPT-Rosalind, our dedicated life sciences model", so "a domain workbench around frontier models rather than a domain model" is half right.

Checked 2026-10-02: research preview in the ChatGPT app; molecular structure, sequence and alignment viewers and an NGS Analysis Workbench; tasks across protein design, small-molecule design and genomics; Explore mode, and Research mode for verified organisation members, with individual access "coming soon".

Two things the averages hide, drawn below: Gemini's ALFWorld score is 85.9 under every method, and WikiSkill is below "no skill" in one cell (Qwen-3.5-4B on OfficeQA, 28.5 against 30.2).

Checked 2026-10-02: the abstract matches (planning, long-term memory and soft offloading tools; branch sampling at decisions picked by context and entropy variation); "accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Track)". The repository's scripts cover Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B; the 14B checkpoint itself was not checked.

51.dnote: undated in the issue; the page was live by Jun 4
notes: Two figures are mixed up. The page gives about 3x for Claude Opus 4 in May 2025 and about 4x for a skilled human researcher after four to eight hours, against about 52x for Claude Mythos Preview in April 2026; "3-4x for skilled humans" joins the two. And it gives the 8x two ways: "8x as much code per quarter as they did from 2021-2025" in its summary, "8x as much code per day as they were in 2024" in the body.

The TechCrunch link is about a different paper: "Automated Researchers Can Reliably Mitigate Alignment Failures" by Anthropic fellow Chen Yueh-Han (the best automated method beats experienced humans within six hours on average, at about $4 an hour of inference against $150 for a researcher).

Checked 2026-10-02 against "When AI builds itself": more than 80% of merged code authored by Claude as of May 2026; 76% on the most open-ended tasks in May 2026; the agents recovered 97% of the gap (two human researchers, about 23%) over 800 hours and about $18,000 of compute; the quote is exact. The Wayback Machine first captured the page on Jun 4, 2026, so it was not new in the window; the {{2026-09-21 issue|n:3e25c17b0d0d813dba03fa81f5d8cc39}} dates it Sep 18.

Checked 2026-10-02 against OpenAI's post (Wayback copy of Sep 1) and CNBC: the proposed shutoff is Nov 12, 2026, "the maximum notice provided by our contract", with no future models; the agreement allows cancelling after a change of control, and OpenAI cites Musk's companies breaking its terms. SpaceX completed its $60 billion purchase of Cursor on Aug 14; Cursor's CEO says OpenAI models serve about 5% of its traffic. Aug 29 to Nov 12 is 75 days, 10.7 weeks (derived).

Checked 2026-10-02: the quote is Jason Hardy's ("We saw upwards of 3x improvement in these operations, where the Vera CPU is allowing for acceleration"); the platform also includes the Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator.
Checked 2026-10-02: Musk's post of Aug 29; transformers at 48 to 60 months; analysts' 66 GW of US data-center demand by 2027. 15 / 66 = 23% (derived), the "large fraction".

Checked 2026-10-02 against the release (Aug 26): every figure and change as stated, including DFlash2 "with local convolution and a candidate selector", max_num_batched_tokens from 8,192 to 16,384, and Transformers 5.15.0.

Checked 2026-10-02 against the LessWrong post (Aug 30) and the authors' page: over 15 runs of 7 days the worm exploited 73.8% of the network and replicated to 61.8%, reaching half the network in about five days; its attempts to edit the IP blacklist were caught at the hypervisor, with no breach of containment. The paper ({{arXiv 2606.03811|https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03811}}) was submitted Jun 2.

Source found on 2026-10-02: {{openai/codex issue #41711|https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/41711}}, "PRIVATE CHAT THREAD EXFILTRATION: Memories exfiltrates local-provider chat content to OpenAI without notice", opened Aug 30. It reports that the memory writer picks a prior rollout without restricting it to the provider that made it, and sends it through the provider of the current session; a controlled capture on Codex 0.150.0-alpha.12.2 showed five items reaching OpenAI's endpoint with analytics off.
Still a user report: the issue is open with two comments as of 2026-10-02, and OpenAI has not confirmed it there.

Checked 2026-10-02: the post (Aug 30) frames it as "value over replacement" for engineers.

followups.t: Nvidia confirms it is buying Hugging Face for $12.93 billion
followups.html: Confirmed on Sep 3, a week after this issue's report that terms were unsigned. Nvidia says Hugging Face "will remain an open platform" and "NVIDIA compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face"; the Hub serves more than 18 million developers and 3 million models ({{Nvidia|https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-to-acquire-hugging-face/}}, {{TechCrunch, Sep 3|https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/03/nvidia-confirms-it-will-buy-hugging-face-for-12-9-billion/}}, covered in the {{next issue|n:3d45c17b0d0d81dca858e1cec21d3314}}).
John Ternus became CEO on Sep 1 and Tim Cook executive chairman, after 15 years as CEO ({{MacRumors|https://www.macrumors.com/2026/09/01/john-ternus-is-now-apple-ceo/}}).

Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 announcement reports 52.6% on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1. Its own setup reproduces the leaderboard's Opus 5 and Fable 5 at 29.0% and 24.7% (against 30.0% and 21.4% here), "within noise" at a standard error of 3.5 to 4.5 points ({{Anthropic|https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-1}}).

followups.t: The 4-bit builds kept following the releases
followups.html: Nvidia's NVFP4 builds of GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next appeared on Hugging Face on Sep 2, 8 and 9 days after the originals ({{nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4|https://huggingface.co/nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4}}, {{nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4|https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4}}, creation dates from the Hugging Face API).

followups.t: GPT-6 Astra shipped, and ARC Prize scored it two ways
followups.html: OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on Sep 3 ({{OpenAI|https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/}}, which refuses automated reading; covered in the {{next issue|n:3d45c17b0d0d81dca858e1cec21d3314}}). ARC Prize scored it 62.7% on ARC-AGI-3 with its standard harness for about $26K, and 99.9% for about $19K with a Provider Adapter harness that keeps the model's opaque reasoning state between requests ({{ARC Prize, Sep 3|https://arcprize.org/blog/astra}}): the same harness question as [[Top stories|t-top|i-harness]].

followups.t: vLLM v0.29.0 makes Model Runner V2 the default
followups.html: 594 commits from 277 contributors (91 new); Model Runner V2 becomes the default for all models ({{release notes|https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.29.0}}, Sep 9).

followups.t: Anthropic's threat report: "sophisticated attacks no longer require sophisticated attackers"
followups.html: Anthropic's September threat intelligence report covers activity it disrupted from December 2025 to August 2026, and its first trend is that AI has collapsed the skill gap between ordinary and sophisticated attackers ({{Anthropic|https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026}}, covered in the {{2026-09-14 issue|n:3db5c17b0d0d8135a34af60966c5ecc1}}; the report carries no date of its own, so it is dated here by that issue).

followups.t: Z.ai: GLM-5.3 built the stack that serves GLM-5.3-Flash
followups.html: Z.ai's "Toward Recursive Self-Improvement: How GLM Built Its Own Inference Infrastructure" reports a production serving system for GLM-5.3-Flash built in 13 days with a 3.22x end-to-end throughput gain, with humans keeping control of objectives ({{Z.ai|https://z.ai/blog/glm-built-its-inference-infrastructure}}, as reported in the {{2026-09-21 issue|n:3e25c17b0d0d813dba03fa81f5d8cc39}}; Z.ai's page renders by script and was not re-read).
